headings.title: Introduction to Oncologic Emergencies
headings.content: Oncologic emergencies are acute, life-threatening complications that can occur directly from cancer growth, tumor metastasis, or as a toxic side effect of systemic therapies like chemotherapy and radiation. These crises can affect nearly any organ system in the body. They demand immediate recognition and rapid medical or surgical intervention to prevent permanent organ damage or death. Nurses working in oncology wards, emergency rooms, and general medical units in Nigeria often serve as the first line of defense, spotting subtle clinical shifts before a patient crashes. Understanding these events means recognizing that cancer is not only a chronic, debilitating disease but can also present with sudden, unpredictable acute episodes.

headings.title: Metabolic Emergencies: Tumor Lysis Syndrome and Hypercalcemia
headings.content:
Metabolic emergencies stem from rapid chemical imbalances caused by cancer cells or their destruction. 

- **Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS)**: Occurs when massive numbers of cancer cells die quickly, usually after starting chemotherapy, dumping intracellular potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids into the bloodstream. This overwhelms the kidneys, causing severe hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and acute uric acid nephropathy.
- **Hypercalcemia of Malignancy**: Frequently triggered by bone metastases or parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) secreted by tumors. Excess calcium enters the bloodstream, leading to profound dehydration, altered mental status, muscle weakness, and cardiac arrhythmias.

headings.title: Structural Emergencies: Spinal Cord Compression and Superior Vena Cava Syndrome
headings.content:
Structural emergencies happen when a growing tumor physically presses on vital organs or major blood vessels.

- **Spinal Cord Compression (MSCC)**: Caused by tumor invasion into the epidural space, pressing against the spinal cord. New-onset back pain, progressive motor weakness, sensory loss, and bowel or bladder dysfunction are classic red flags requiring urgent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and corticosteroids.
- **Superior Vena Cava Syndrome (SVCS)**: Results from external compression or thrombosis of the superior vena cava, blocking venous return from the head, neck, and upper extremities. Patients present with facial edema, neck vein distension, and dyspnea.

headings.title: Hematologic Emergencies: Febrile Neutropenia and Hyperleukocytosis
headings.content:
Hematologic emergencies involve dangerous alterations in blood cell counts, leaving patients vulnerable to overwhelming infection or stroke-like microvascular blockages.

- **Febrile Neutropenia**: Defined as an oral temperature of 38.3°C or higher, or a sustained temperature of 38.0°C for over an hour, alongside an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) below 500 cells/mm³. Because standard inflammatory signs may be absent due to low white cell counts, fever can be the only indicator of a deadly systemic infection.
- **Hyperleukocytosis**: Occurs when white blood cell counts skyrocket, often above 100,000 cells/mm³ in leukemias, causing blood hyperviscosity and slowing microcirculation in the lungs and brain.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Early Recognition
headings.content: Spotting an oncologic emergency relies on vigilance, baseline knowledge, and routine physical assessments. Nurses must actively monitor vital signs, intake and output, and neurological status in all patients undergoing active cancer treatment. A common clinical mistake is attributing new fatigue, mild confusion, or generalized aches solely to the cancer's progression or normal chemotherapy side effects. Instead, nurses should maintain a high index of suspicion, screening for changes in breathing patterns, urine output, and peripheral circulation during every shift handoff.

headings.title: Acute Management and Interventions
headings.content:
When an oncologic emergency strikes, immediate stabilization takes precedence over diagnostic confirmation. 

| Emergency | Immediate Intervention |
| --- | --- |
| **Febrile Neutropenia** | Draw blood cultures and start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within one hour |
| **Tumor Lysis Syndrome** | Aggressive IV hydration and allopurinol or rasburicase to lower uric acid |
| **Spinal Cord Compression** | Administer high-dose corticosteroids and prepare for urgent radiation or surgery |
| **Hypercalcemia** | IV normal saline hydration combined with loop diuretics or bisphosphonates |

Delaying treatment while waiting for laboratory test results can lead to catastrophic patient outcomes.
